mu[3] <- exp(c+e[3] + D[1]*e[2] + D[2]*e[1]);

mu[5] <- exp(c+e[5] + D[1]*e[4] + D[2]*e[3]+D[3]*e[2]+D[4]*e[1]);
mu[6] <- exp(c+e[6] + D[1]*e[5] + D[2]*e[4]+D[3]*e[3]+D[4]*e[2]+D[5]*e[1]);
mu[7] <- exp(c+e[7] + D[1]*e[6] + D[2]*e[5]+D[3]*e[4]+D[4]*e[3]+D[5]*e[2]+D[6]*e[1]);
mu[8] <- exp(c+e[8] + D[1]*e[7] + D[2]*e[6]+D[3]*e[5]+D[4]*e[4]+D[5]*e[3]+D[6]*e[2]+D[7]*e[1]);

and so on




Below is my code:


library(rstan)

cat("Stan version:", stan_version(), "\n")
stanmodelcode <- "

data {
int<lower=0> N;
int y[N];
}

parameters {
real<lower=0, upper=0.5> d;
real c;
real<lower=0> sig2;
vector[N] e;


}

transformed parameters {
vector[N] mu;
vector[N] arg;
vector[N] D;


for (i in 1:N){

D[i]<-exp((lgamma(d+i)-lgamma(d))-lgamma(i+1));


}



for (i in 1:N) {

arg[i]<-c+e[i];

k<- i-1;

for (j in 1:(i-1)){


arg[i]<-arg[i]+e[j]*D[k];
k<- k-1;
}


mu[i]<-exp(arg[i]);
}



}


model {

c~normal(0,10);
d ~ uniform(0,0.5);
sig2~gamma(3,1);
e~normal(0,sig2);
y ~ poisson(mu);

}



generated quantities {
vector[N] log_lik;
 real dev; // deviance
 
  for (n in 1:N){
    log_lik[n] <- poisson_log (y[n],mu[n]);
  }


        dev <- 0;
        for ( n in 1:N ) {
            dev <- dev + (-2) * poisson_log (y[n],mu[n]);
        }
  

  
}

"

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] seeking help with my loop, thanks
parts:
I don't see what you're asking. You define k in the loop.
If you meant "declare" rather than "define", you can declare
it as a local variable at the top of whatever block it's
defined in.

> ...

I think this'll do it without the k:

vector[N] e;
vector[N-1] D; // looks like this is one shorter than mu and e

vector[N] mu;
mu <- c + e; // takes care of leading two terms

for (n in 2:N)
for (m in 1:(n-1))
mu[n] <- mu[n] + D[m] * e[n - m];

mu <- exp(mu);

But you should definitely double-check it by running the loop by
hand or even better by writing the calculation of mu as a function (of
c, e, and D), and testing that for some test cases.

It's probably also possible to do this with dot products of
slices of vectors (by reversing either e or D --- I didn't ry
to work it out).

We don't generally recommend computing deviances and usually
do recommend consider very carefully considering the
dispersion properties of the Poisson and moving to an
overdispersed count distribution like negative binomial if
the assumptions of the Poisson aren't satisfied.

We have a Poisson defined on the log scale,

y ~ poisson_log(alpha)

which is the same as

y ~ poisson(exp(alpha))

so you shouldn't ever be exponentiating a parameter for the
Poisson.

We also strongly recommend indenting so it's easier to read
programs.

- Bob
